lines.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for being here. Let us move to item four on our agenda: the protection of our network.

Presenting today is Daniel Hale, our Chief Information Security Officer. Daniel has led our security for six years. Before he joined us, he spent twelve years protecting the networks of a national bank and a large hospital group. This year he led our response to two attempted break-ins, and both were stopped before any harm was done. He holds the main professional certifications in his field.

Daniel is asking the board for two point four million dollars to strengthen the protection of our warehouses and our head office. Our insurer and our largest customer both expect this protection to be in place within the year. We will hear his five slides and ask our questions along the way. The board will decide on the budget today.
Thank you, Margaret. Good morning, everyone.

layout.text: Why we are here today
Our 12 warehouses and head office run on one network: orders, scanners, trucks and payroll
This year we stopped two attempted break-ins into that network
Our insurer requires stronger protection before renewal in 10 months
Our largest customer requires the same in its new contract

scenes._layoutNote: s1.num1 is split into value and caption from the v1.1 text '$2.4 million: budget request for approval today'.

narration.text: I will keep this short and clear, because I am asking you for a decision today. Everything we do runs on one network. Orders come in, the scanners in our twelve warehouses track every pallet, our trucks get their routes, and our fourteen hundred people get paid. If that network stops, the company stops. This year, we stopped two attempted break-ins into that network. Both were caught early, and no harm was done. But attackers are getting better, and we need to stay ahead of them. Two outside parties have also told us what they expect. Our insurer will renew our cyber insurance in ten months only if stronger protection is in place. And our largest customer has written the same requirement into its new contract. So today, I am asking for two point four million dollars to put that protection in place. On the next four slides, I will show you what we will build, what it costs, and when it will be ready.

layout.text: A firewall at every site keeps warehouse machines apart from office computers
All 12 warehouses connect to our data centre at head office
One internet connection, at head office, watched day and night
Staff at home or on the road use secure remote access

narration.text: Let me show you how the network will look. Picture our head office in the middle of this diagram. Our main data centre sits there. All twelve warehouses connect to that data centre. That is the line you see from each warehouse to the centre. At every site, we put a firewall. Think of a firewall as a locked door with a guard. It decides what may come in and go out, and it keeps the warehouse machines apart from the office computers. So if one computer is infected, the problem stays in that room. Then we have one connection to the internet, at head office, and our security team watches it day and night. Finally, people who work from home or on the road connect through secure remote access. They get in only after we have checked who they are.

layout.text: What the $2.4 million pays for

layout.caption: Firewalls for 13 sites, with 3 years of support

narration.text: Now to the money, and where the two point four million dollars goes. The first line is the firewalls for all thirteen sites, with three years of support: seven hundred and eighty thousand dollars. The largest line is round-the-clock monitoring for two years: nine hundred and sixty thousand dollars. For that, a team of specialists watches our network every hour of every day, and they can close a door within minutes if something looks wrong. We could not build that team ourselves for this price. Next is secure remote access for all fourteen hundred staff: three hundred and ten thousand dollars. And finally, installation and staff training: three hundred and fifty thousand dollars. Most break-ins start with a fake email, so training our people is some of the best value on this page. Together, that is two point four million dollars.

narration.text: So when will this be ready? The work comes in three phases. Phase one, design and ordering, takes two months. Phase two, installing the firewalls at all thirteen sites, takes five months. Phase three, setting up the monitoring and training our staff, takes four months. Altogether, we are ready in eight months. Our insurance renewal is in ten months, so that gives us two months of margin. Why does the timing matter? Because the risk is real, and it is expensive. If our warehouses stop for a single day, we lose about one point two million dollars in shipments. That is half of this request, gone in one day. And an attack rarely stops things for only one day. If we start today, we are protected well before the renewal. If we wait another quarter, we miss it.

layout.text: The decision today
A firewall at all 13 sites and one watched internet connection
24-hour monitoring of our network for two years
Secure remote access and training for all staff
Ready in 8 months, before our insurance renewal

narration.text: Let me bring this together. Every one of our thirteen sites gets a firewall, and we keep a single, watched connection to the internet. Specialists monitor our network around the clock for two years. Everyone who works away from the office connects securely, and all staff learn to spot fake emails. The whole plan costs two point four million dollars, and it is ready in eight months, before our insurance renewal. If we wait, we face a much higher insurance premium, or no cover at all, and the contract with our largest customer is at risk. I am confident this is the right plan for this company: the right size, at the right time. So I am asking the board to approve two point four million dollars today. Thank you.
